name: Atahan Kılıç
availability: Open to full-time roles · Munich / EU
tagline: I build systems that have to be right — then make them feel effortless.
about: AI & full-stack software engineer in Munich. I build AI products end to end: the agent and LLM layer, the React and React Native front ends people touch, and the back ends that keep the answers honest.

Since April 2026 I've been building BugSense for my M.Sc. thesis at TUM: the software of an AI-based UTI diagnostic. A mini-incubator images a paper cassette, a model proposes infection, species and bacterial load, and a clinician approves, edits or rejects every result before it goes anywhere. Instead of a 48–72 hour lab culture, the answer comes back the same day. Under EU law that makes it both an in-vitro diagnostic (IVDR) and a high-risk AI system (AI Act).

In November 2026 I took first place twice in a row: in the Reonic challenge with OnlyPanels (solar, battery and heat-pump designs an expert planner would sign), and at Sphere Forge #1 with an agent that turns a design brief and eight rendered views into a STEP solid.

Alongside the thesis I'm a working student at CHECK24, building the customer area and aftersales for CHECK24 Autoteile across PHP/Symfony, React and SQL. Before that: a year and a half at NextAim shipping web, iOS and Android apps with AI chat on Azure-hosted LLMs, and two and a half years at HAVELSAN on NATO-standard simulators and real-time C++.
now: M.Sc. Informatics @ TUM — thesis on BugSense

projects.title: BugSense
projects.blurb: The website I built for BugSense, an AI-assisted UTI diagnostic (that's the live link). My M.Sc. thesis is the device software behind it: re-architected as a regulation-ready SaMD under IEC 62304 / ISO 14971, with on-device acquisition, cloud inference, audit logging and clinician reporting. The thesis isn't public.

architecture.summary: My M.Sc. thesis: the software behind BugSense, a culture-based UTI test. A mini-incubator images the test cassette over several hours, an AI model proposes a diagnosis, and a healthcare professional reviews it before it is released. That makes it an in-vitro diagnostic device under the IVDR and a high-risk AI system under the EU AI Act. The thesis builds those requirements into the architecture instead of documenting them afterwards. (The live link is the public website; the thesis code isn't public.)
parts: clients
clinical app (review and release), viewer app (released results only), the mini-incubator sending time-series images; on web, desktop and mobile
core service
accounts and organisations, run and image intake, review and release, the audit trail
inference
a separate worker running the frozen model: ONNX Runtime, CPU only, the same in every deployment
data
PostgreSQL and image storage, behind one storage interface
decisions: One codebase, two first-class deployments: a multi-tenant cloud run by BugSense, and a self-contained on-premises install bundled with the desktop app. The customer chooses; both get the same scope.

PostgreSQL in both, because the guarantees live inside the database: tenant isolation is row-level security on tenant_id, so the database refuses cross-tenant reads even if the application gets it wrong.
A tamper-evident audit log: each entry hashes its own content plus the previous entry's hash, and signed checkpoints use a key kept outside the database.
The model version is the whole pipeline: the digest of a manifest covering the weights, preprocessing, frame selection and abstain threshold. Change any of them and it is a new model version.
One inference per test, committed only once a proposal is durably stored. A failed dispatch retries the same stored image series, within a budget.

The AI only proposes. Its fields have the same shape as the released result, so a reviewer changes values, never structure. The model may abstain, and its confidence is stored but never shown until clinical evidence supports showing it.
The research question: which regulatory requirements can the architecture itself guarantee, and which stay organisational or clinical tasks?
Built with an AI coding agent working from a structured knowledge base of decisions, requirements, risks and rules.

projects.title: OnlyPanels
projects.blurb: Solar, battery, wallbox and heat-pump designs the way an expert planner would propose them. It fuses open data about a home (3D roofs, aerial photos, sun, shade, census); a deterministic engine, not the LLM, sets every number.

architecture.summary: Won first place in the Reonic challenge 2026. The finding behind it: 59% of solar requests match another customer's field for field, yet in 99% of those the experts still designed differently, by 6.3 kWp on average. They knew the roof, the shade, the street. So the work is gathering context, and a deterministic engine designs from it.
parts: web/
React + MapLibre + three.js: click a house in Munich, its 3D roof with fitted modules; nine optional homeowner pages; the planner's desk (design, cost, offer, proof)
engine/
solar and battery sizes learned per installer from 1,041 past projects, catalog snapping, rules for heat pump, wallbox, grants and German energy law
simulation
hourly own-power and savings on real Munich weather years from PVGIS, checked against HTW Berlin values
api/
FastAPI; Claude reads the roof photo, the planner's sentence box and drives a voice agent through MCP tools, with ElevenLabs for speech
decisions: The language model never produces a design number: the engine does. Without keys everything runs on rules.
Every fact is tagged customer, measured, found or assumed; assumed facts must be confirmed before an offer goes out.
The review reruns the engine at the edges of each guessed answer and lists which one would still move the design.
Nothing leaves the homeowner's browser before Send, and they choose what goes; without an address it still extracts facts from words.
Scored once on 276 held-out projects: solar mean error 2.65 kWp against 3.06 (same design for all) and 4.02 (rule of thumb).

projects.title: Prompt-to-CAD
projects.blurb: Turns a design brief and eight rendered views of a mechanical part into a STEP solid. A deterministic OpenCascade pipeline carves a valid shape first, then LLM agents write CadQuery and check it against the views.

architecture.summary: Won first place at Sphere Forge #1. For each part the input is a written brief, facts.json (bounding box, volume, hole inventory) and eight orthographic views; the output is one solid in millimetres, ranked on nine hidden parts. Deterministic geometry first, a model only proposes, and a judge decides.
parts: pipeline
a box cut through view by view along silhouettes rebuilt from lines and arcs, then listed holes, mouths, pockets, rounds and curved recesses, each kept only if it fits
agents
one agent per part writes CadQuery, runs ./check against facts.json and the views, and replaces the pipeline's file only with a better candidate
judge
verify.py and judge.py score a solid against the inputs without ground truth; a 266-part local eval set with ground truth for development
dashboard
inputs, our solid after every step, the diff against the truth in 3D
decisions: Every part has a valid file from the first second: boxes first, checkpointed writes, never a 0 from a crash or a kill.
Build for unseen parts: no threshold chosen on the nine practice parts.
Models compared by measurement: Claude Opus, several OpenAI models and open-weight VLMs served with vLLM on RTX PRO 6000s.
Shipped as a Docker image through CI to the organisers' registry; a push to main is a submission.

projects.title: North Star
projects.blurb: Real-time collaborative ideation workspace: post-its, structure, competitor feature matrices — rendered in a 3D ASCII aesthetic.

architecture.summary: A static single-page app on GitHub Pages with no server of its own. The browser talks to Firebase directly, and Firebase's security rules decide who can read and write what.
parts: src/data/
the only layer that talks to Firebase, so another backend swap stays contained
src/three/
React Three Fiber backdrop with a hand-written ASCII effect, plus the welcome intro
src/views/
the canvas: a DOM layer that pans and zooms, holding cards, links, matrices, tables, kanbans and documents
rules
firestore.rules and database.rules.json, tested against the local emulators
decisions: Firebase, chosen for longevity: InstantDB was shutting down, free Supabase projects pause, and Convex bills every cursor update.
Firestore holds everything persistent. Realtime Database only carries presence and cursors, because it is cheap and has onDisconnect.
Hybrid rendering: WebGL for the backdrop and transitions, DOM for anything you read or edit. The ASCII effect never touches text.
Only what is on screen gets drawn; a dense, zoomed-out matrix paints into a 2D canvas.
Plain-path routing on GitHub Pages: the build copies index.html to 404.html, so every deep link boots the app.

projects.title: Steward
projects.blurb: Talk to your building. Ask where something is, how to get there for you (wheelchair, trolley, no lifts) and what changes when a lift closes; facility managers edit the building by chat or voice, always propose → confirm → apply. 280 buildings. A deterministic geometry/graph core computes every answer, the LLM only speaks.

architecture.summary: A request goes frontend → api → agents → core. The agents decide what to compute, a deterministic core computes it. No agent states a room, distance or route that didn't come out of a tool.
parts: frontend/
React + Vite + three.js: map, building search, plan view, the Guide chat and Edit mode
backend/api/
FastAPI: sessions, Supabase persistence, speech in and out, the live building state
backend/agents/
the Claude agents: Guide (find, route, react, edit), Builder (edits a building), Creator (drafts one from floor plans)
backend/core/
no LLM, no HTTP: route graph, geometry, solvers, access profiles, edits, plan import
decisions: Dependencies point one way: core never imports agents or api.
One tool layer for every agent: building_overview, search, room_facts, find_route, find_nearest and the edit tools are plain Python functions exposed as tools.
Access needs (wheelchair, trolley, no lifts) are routing profiles on the graph, so a closed lift reroutes deterministically.
Edits go propose → confirm → apply: a draft is validated before it changes the shared building.
Without an API key the Guide runs offline, so the app always starts.

projects.title: SharkSight
projects.blurb: 10,128 customer comments become prioritized, evidence-linked requirements for the next BMW 1/5/7 Series. The AI proposes, the PM decides, every step lands in an append-only audit trail.

architecture.summary: An evidence base runs through a staged AI pipeline and comes out as scored, evidence-linked requirements. The AI proposes, the product manager decides, and every step lands in an append-only audit trail.
parts: evidence
customer comments, a customer study, sales figures, option price lists and about 900 cited web sources
backend/
FastAPI and PostgreSQL with pgvector; every pipeline step is an agent with its own model, effort, spend cap and switch
frontend/
React + three.js, five pages in the PM's order: Evidence, Structure, Definition, Prioritize, Document
audit
append-only; the database itself refuses edits and deletions
decisions: Two real-date checkpoints, JAN 26 and JUL 26. The second builds on the first, so needs that are new, held, stronger or weaker are visible.
Every requirement has a customer metric and a target ladder (baseline, threshold, target, stretch); each number is marked cited, projected, assumption or gap.
A score for every requirement × car line × market, with its factors (customer, business, future) visible, sorted into Must, Should and Could.
When new evidence moves a score against a band the PM confirmed, the AI doesn't change it. It raises an upgrade or downgrade proposal with its cause.
Deployed on Render, database on Neon.

projects.title: Harmos
projects.blurb: An AI-native CAD platform. Every capability is a typed command; the GUI is just another client of the API the agent uses. Geometry addressed by predicate selectors, verified by the engine.

architecture.summary: A CAD application whose main operator is an AI. The engine owns all state; every client, the AI included, talks to it over one versioned protocol, so the GUI has no privileged path.
parts: engine/
Python: protocol server, document model, command registry, op-log, B-Rep kernel adapter, verification and the agent loop
schemas/
the contract as data: protocol, rejection classes, selector vocabulary. The engine loads it, the client generates its types from it
client/
pnpm workspace: protocol types, a three.js viewer and the React editor, fed per-body GLB deltas
docs/
ADRs, requirements, hazards and the worklog; make check decides when a change is finished
decisions: Every capability is a typed, named, serializable command, applied in atomic transactions against a known base version.
Geometry is addressed by predicates ("the planar face whose normal ≈ +Z"), not kernel IDs, so intent survives a rebuild.
The agent loop: orient → propose → validate → evaluate → verify → commit. Validation, the kernel and verification fail separately, and each returns a structured rejection, never prose.
Measurement replaces belief: the agent asks the engine for a wall thickness and gets a number with a unit.
The agent commits to its own branch, never to main.

projects.title: TATE AI
projects.blurb: Teachers dictate a lesson summary; Gemini turns it into structured class and student records. Field-tested with real teachers, SUS 83/100.

architecture.summary: A teacher dictates a summary after class. Speech recognition turns it into text, and Gemini turns the transcript into a structured lesson record.
parts: app/
Expo Router screens, plus api/chat+api.ts, the one network call: a server route that proxies to Gemini
components/
recorder, transcript editor and AI summary; class, subject, student, lecture and schedule views
lib/chat/
the system prompt that shapes the record: objective, topics, methods, materials, homework, observations, absences, notes
mock-data/
classes, students and timelines in memory: a prototype, no persistence yet
decisions: The Gemini key stays on the server: the app calls its own API route, never Gemini directly.
The teacher can correct the transcript before it is summarized.
One Expo codebase for iOS, Android and the web.
Field-tested with real teachers: SUS 83/100.

projects.title: Routemaxxing
projects.blurb: An LLM router trained from real request logs that show only which model ran. Rebuilt 1,000 rows into 10,845 turns and shipped a cost–quality frontier.

architecture.summary: The logs show only which model ran: no outputs, no token counts. The router reconstructs what was actually billed, then routes each task to the cheapest model whose expected quality matches.
parts: rebuild
each row is a whole trajectory; splitting the model-produced runs gives 10,845 billed calls (grouping by opening text gave 953 groups, 19 of them mixed-model)
ledger
cache-aware input + output cost, tokens estimated as chars / 4; logged spend $278.36
router
features from the first request only; per model it estimates cost, tokens, a quality proxy, uncertainty and support
evaluation
five-fold cross-fitting, task-grouped folds, a doubly robust estimator and paired bootstrap intervals
decisions: A whole trajectory stays on one model family, so a mid-task switch never throws away the cache.
Recommended policy v4: $138.00, 50.4% below logged spend, quality +0.0004 (95% interval −0.0041 … +0.0048): no detected change.
v5 is cheaper ($120.48), but its GPT decision rests on 20 trajectories, so it isn't the recommendation.
Transparent lexical and structural nearest-neighbour matching, no black-box model.
